1885-10-08.text: The Bad Lands Cow Boy is of the opinion that the range is not badly damaged by fire but that there is no "grass to loan."
1885-10-08.summary: The Cow Boy judged that the fall prairie fires had not badly damaged the Bad Lands range, though there was no grass to spare.
1885-10-08.credit: The Bad Lands Cow Boy is of the opinion
1885-10-08.why: Daily Yellowstone Journal (Miles City) of Saturday Oct 10, 1885 cites the Bad Lands Cow Boy; the only Cow Boy issue in between was Oct 8 (missing), and the surviving Oct 1 issue has no such remark.

1885-10-08.text: One furrow, plowed for twenty-five miles along the divide next to the Bad Lands, saved the Bad Land ranges between Medora and Beauer Creek from serious damage by the prairie fires. The Cow Boy now proposes that the whole of the Bad Lands be protected next season by double furrows on the east and west sides.
1885-10-08.summary: A 25-mile fire furrow had saved the ranges between Medora and Beaver Creek, and the Cow Boy proposed double furrows around the whole Bad Lands next season.
1885-10-08.why: Hope Pioneer of Oct 23, 1885 summarizes a Cow Boy proposal. The surviving Oct 1, 15 and 22 issues have nothing on fire furrows, leaving the missing Oct 8 issue as the likely source.

1885-11-05.text: The Bad Lands Cow Boy of last week says of the Marquis de Mores extensive slaughtering house: The slaughter house did the last killing of the season Saturday, and Monday morning the butchers all started for Chicago. There will be considerable work in the ice season, but aside from this there will probably be no steady work at the slaughter house until next June.
1885-11-05.summary: The Marquis de Mores's Medora slaughter house finished its season's killing and the butchers left for Chicago, with little steady work expected until June apart from ice harvesting.
1885-11-05.credit: The Bad Lands Cow Boy of last week says of the Marquis de Mores extensive slaughtering house:
1885-11-05.why: Jamestown Weekly Alert of Thursday Nov 12, 1885 quotes 'The Bad Lands Cow Boy of last week', i.e. the missing Nov 5 issue. The surviving Oct 29 issue does not carry it.

1885-11-05.text: Medora (Dakota) Cowboy: The bulls of the quarter circle diamond, L C and Maltese cross brands have been gatherer and will be wintered near the Big Plateau, five miles down the river, where an abundance of hay has been provided.
1885-11-05.summary: The bulls of the Quarter Circle Diamond, LC and Maltese Cross (Roosevelt's) outfits were gathered to winter on hay at the Big Plateau, five miles down the Little Missouri.
1885-11-05.why: Austin Weekly Statesman of Nov 19, 1885 credits the 'Medora (Dakota) Cowboy'. The surviving Oct 1 issue said the bulls 'will' be gathered and the Nov 26 issue says they are 'now in good fix'; this 'have been gathered' item, with its 'five miles down the river' detail, is in none of the surviving Oct 15, 22, 29 or Nov 19 issues. It must come from a missing issue (Oct 8, Nov 5 or Nov 12); given the time needed to reach Texas, Nov 5 is the best guess. The St. Johns Herald (Ariz.) reprinted the same item on Nov 26, 1885.

1885-11-12.text: J. B. Walker, of Medora, has skipped leaving a number of unpaid debts behind him.—Bad Lands Cow Boy.
1885-11-12.summary: J. B. Walker, the new landlord of Medora's Metropolitan hotel, skipped town leaving unpaid debts.
1885-11-12.why: Daily Yellowstone Journal of Saturday Nov 14, 1885 credits the Bad Lands Cow Boy. Both Cow Boy issues before it (Nov 12 and Nov 5) are missing; the surviving Nov 19 issue says 'Nothing has been heard of J. B. Walker', a follow-up to this report. Nov 12 is the most recent issue, but Nov 5 cannot be ruled out.

1885-11-12.text:
The party that went down the river last Wednesday to persuade the Indians to stay on their reservation, returned Saturday. They found but little to do as only ten or a dozen of the Indians remained and they were fast making preparations to follow their brethern, who had left for their reservation. No fear is entertained of their return as they consider cow boys "bad medicine" and are by this time thoroughly convinced that their presence is not desired in the cow country.
—Medora Cow Boy.
1885-11-12.summary: A party of cowboys sent down the Little Missouri to push a band of Indians back to their reservation found most had already left.
1885-11-12.why: Daily Yellowstone Journal of Saturday Nov 14, 1885 credits the 'Medora Cow Boy'. A Nov 4 dispatch reported the stockmen would send a party of cowboys on Thursday to drive off the Indians, which puts this report of their return in the Nov 12 issue. The surviving Nov 19 issue lacks it, and the Nov 26 issue follows up ('since the party went down the river to remove them').

1885-11-12.text: The Bad Lands Cowboy states that J. B. Walker "skipped out" and left debts of about $1,000.
1885-11-12.summary: A second report of the same Cow Boy item puts J. B. Walker's unpaid debts at about $1,000.
1885-11-12.credit: The Bad Lands Cowboy states that
1885-11-12.why: St. Paul Daily Globe of Nov 17, 1885 paraphrases the Bad Lands Cowboy on J. B. Walker. It is the same news as the Yellowstone Journal's Nov 14 reprint, from a missing issue (Nov 12, or possibly Nov 5); the surviving Nov 19 issue only follows up.

1885-11-12.text: The Bad Lands Cowboy says that all the Black Hills wants is a railroad and a new moral character for its business men.
1885-11-12.summary: The Cow Boy jibed that the Black Hills needed only a railroad and a new moral character for its businessmen.
1885-11-12.why: Rock Island Argus of Nov 24, 1885 is the earliest of several papers carrying this Bad Lands Cowboy quip (also Pembina Pioneer Express Nov 27, Superior Times Dec 26, Sedalia Bazoo Jan 19, 1886). It is not in any surviving issue from October to January, so it most likely came from the missing Nov 12 issue (Nov 5 is also possible).

1885-12-10.text: Speaking of the organization of Billings county, the Bad Lands Cow Boy says: "There is said to be a movement on foot to defeat county organization, but it cannot legally be successful. As we understand the law, all responsibility on the part of the governor ceases as soon as he receives a petition for organization, containining the names of 150 qualified voters. After this, there is no option on his part. He must call an election of officers to hold office until the next regular election. There has been a delay somewhere, but we can see no possible legal way to stop the organization of the county. Not more than five persons refused to sign the petition, so that the movement was practically unanimous."
1885-12-10.summary: The Cow Boy argued that a reported move to block Billings County's organization could not legally succeed, since the governor had to call an election once he had a petition of 150 voters.
1885-12-10.credit: Speaking of the organization of Billings county, the Bad Lands Cow Boy says:
1885-12-10.why: Bismarck Weekly Tribune of Dec 18, 1885 quotes the Bad Lands Cow Boy on Billings county organization. The passage is in none of the surviving Nov 19, 26, Dec 3 or Dec 17 issues, leaving the missing Dec 10 issue.

1886-01-07.text: The Bad Lands Cow Boy says: A close estimate of the amount of deer shipped from Medora this winter is 30,000 pounds, This equals about 600 saddles and is probably not over two thirds of the actual number killed tributary to Medora.
1886-01-07.summary: About 30,000 pounds of deer, some 600 saddles, had been shipped from Medora that winter, perhaps two-thirds of the deer killed in the area.
1886-01-07.credit: The Bad Lands Cow Boy says:
1886-01-07.why: Jamestown Weekly Alert of Jan 14, 1886 quotes 'The Bad Lands Cow Boy says'. The most recent Cow Boy before it was the missing Jan 7 issue; the surviving Dec 17, 24 and 31 issues do not carry the estimate.

1886-03-04.text: An agreement signed by thirty-eight voters, and too long to publish, was brought into the Cow Boy office Tuesday night. In very plain terms it agrees to a combined opposition to anyone attempting to build or grade roads at the public expense after the county election. All agree that when they want roads built they will do it themselves, and will not call on the county to pay for them.—Medora Cow Boy.
1886-03-04.summary: Thirty-eight Billings County voters signed an agreement opposing any road building at public expense after the county election.
1886-03-04.why: Daily Yellowstone Journal (Miles City) of Saturday Mar 6, 1886, two days after the missing Mar 4 issue, credits the 'Medora Cow Boy'; The New North-West (Deer Lodge) reprinted it Mar 19 as from the 'Medora Cowboy'. The agreement followed the Billings county nominating convention of Mar 1 ('Tuesday night' = Mar 2), and it is not in the surviving Feb 25, Mar 11 or Mar 18 issues.

1886-03-04.text: The Medora Cowboy says cattle on the northern ranges have not wintered as well as those near the Hills, and the loss will be about 5 per cent.
1886-03-04.summary: The Cow Boy estimated winter cattle losses on the northern ranges at about 5 percent, worse than near the Black Hills.
1886-03-04.why: A Dakota news column dated Mar 18, 1886 (Wahpeton Times; also Reporter and Farmer, Warner Sun, De Smet Leader, and the Cow Boy's own ready-print page of Mar 18) quotes 'The Medora Cowboy'. The estimate is not in the surviving Feb 25 or Mar 11 local columns, so it most likely came from the missing Mar 4 issue.

1886-03-04.text: It is certainly to be hoped that the International Range Association will carry out its plans in reference to infectious diseases and the selling of cattle especially. It is proposed by a rigid system of quarantine to be absolutely certain that no diseased animal gets into the range country. In the matter of selling cattle it is proposed to do away with middlemen as much as possible, have equal freight rates for all shippers, be they large or small, and to break the grip of the Chicago dressed beef men on the cattle market.—Bad Lands Cowboy.
1886-03-04.summary: The Cow Boy backed the International Range Association's plans for strict quarantine against cattle disease and for cutting out middlemen and the Chicago dressed-beef men.
1886-03-04.why: Hoof and Horn (Prescott, Ariz.) of Mar 25, 1886 credits the Bad Lands Cowboy. The paragraph is not in the surviving Feb 4 to Mar 18 issues (the Mar 11 issue has a different editorial on the International Range Association). The most recent missing issue in reach is Mar 4; Jan 7 is a remoter possibility.

1886-05-27.text: THE Bad Lands Cow Boy says Theodore Roosevelt does his full day's work with the rest of the men, and except for the big spectacles, would pass for a cow puncher anywhere.
1886-05-27.summary: The Cow Boy reported that Theodore Roosevelt did a full day's work alongside his men and, but for his big spectacles, would pass for a cowpuncher anywhere.
1886-05-27.credit: THE Bad Lands Cow Boy says
1886-05-27.why: The River Press (Fort Benton, Mont.) of Wednesday Jun 2, 1886 is the earliest of three Montana papers carrying this (New North-West, Deer Lodge, Jun 4; Bozeman Weekly Chronicle, Jun 9). It is not in the surviving May 6, May 13 or Jun 10 issues. The source is the missing May 27 issue, the most recent before Jun 2; the missing May 20 issue is also possible.

1886-06-03.text: Cowboy: At no time since cattle were first put into the Bad Lands has there been such urgent need of rain as at present. The grass is not yet half grown and the chances for any hay at all are remarkrbly slim. Grass has not only not grown a particle in the last two weeks, but in many places has begun to cure, thus putting a stop to any future growth. There is no disguising the fact that rain must come soon and plentifully if we have even a half crop of grass.
1886-06-03.summary: Drought had stunted the Bad Lands grass, and the Cow Boy warned that without heavy rain there would not be even half a hay crop.
1886-06-03.why: Livingston Enterprise of Saturday Jun 12, 1886 runs this in its exchange column under 'Cowboy:'. The Bad Lands subject identifies the Bad Lands Cow Boy, but the credit is abbreviated. It is not in the surviving May 13, Jun 10 or Jun 17 issues, so it most likely came from the missing Jun 3 issue (late May issues are also missing).

1886-06-24.text: Bad Lands Cow Boy: Work at the slaughter house will begin July 1. Cattle will then be in good condition to kill. In spite of reports to the contrary from other parts of the range country, beef seems to be at least two weeks earlier this year than last.
1886-06-24.summary: The Medora slaughter house was to start the season's killing on July 1, with range beef ripening at least two weeks earlier than in 1885.
1886-06-24.why: Bismarck Weekly Tribune of Jul 2, 1886 credits the Bad Lands Cow Boy. The wording is not in the surviving Jun 10, Jun 17 or Jul 1 issues (Jun 10 said only that the slaughter house would open 'about July 1'), so it comes from the missing Jun 24 issue.

1886-06-24.text: A number of years ago, a certain cavalry station began losing horses very fast. Scarcely a day passed that one or more troopers were not "set afoot." Suspicion finally lit upon a ranchman living near the fort and several horses in his possession were positively identified as belonging to the soldiers. The ranchman showed bills of sale, however, for all his horses and as all were branded with his own brand, which was 108, and no other brand or blotch was visible, nothing could be done. Some of the soldiers were so positive they recognized their horses, that they were given permission to watch the ranchman. After several weeks of weary spying they saw him, one dark night, go to the fort and lead out the best horse in the company through an unguarded door. Following him back to his ranch, they witnessed through a crack in his barn, the transformation scene by which the US brand was "dematerialized" into 108. A figure 1 was added before the US, the top of the U was brought over and closed, the two ends of the S connected, a hot iron run deftly over the parts of the US not already doctored, a bill of sale was filled out, which had already been signed by a partner of the "honest ranchman" and the transfer was complete. Unless the whole operation had been overseen, it is doubtful if any court in the universe would have returned the horse to the government. We are glad to see that the 108 brand is not represented in the Montana brand book.--Medora (Dak.) Cow-Boy.
1886-06-24.summary: A tale of a horse thief who turned the army's US brand into '108', ending with the Cow Boy's relief that no 108 brand appears in the Montana brand book.
1886-06-24.why: Hoof and Horn (Prescott, Ariz.) of Jul 15, 1886 credits the 'Medora (Dak.) Cow-Boy'. The item refers to the Montana brand book, which the surviving Jun 17 issue says was just then being circulated; it is not in the surviving Jun 17, Jul 1 or Jul 8 issues, so the missing Jun 24 issue is the likely source.

1886-07-29.text: Mandan Pioneer: We gather from the Cow Boy that the Marquis de Mores recently lost a couple of rings. He has received the following letter: "Mr. Marquis Demors I understand that you lost two finger rings one has three sets in it and the other one has several letters in it but a plain ring and if you want to git them you can have them by putting a reword in the cow boy paper if it suts then you can git them." The marquis properly replied that he was not in the habit of doing business that way.
1886-07-29.summary: The Marquis de Mores lost two rings and got a misspelled letter offering them back for a reward advertised in the Cow Boy, which he refused.
1886-07-29.credit: Mandan Pioneer: We gather from the Cow Boy that
1886-07-29.why: Bismarck Weekly Tribune of Aug 6, 1886 quotes the Mandan Pioneer, which 'gather[s] from the Cow Boy' this story. It is in none of the surviving July issues (Jul 1 to 22), so it came from a missing issue, most likely Jul 29 given the second-hand route (Aug 5 is also possible).

1886-08-12.text: The Northern Pacific has made an average reduction of fifty per cent. on all stock rates east of Mandan. This cut is made to meet a reduction by the Manitoba and at the instance of the railroad commissioners that the rate be equalized with those in Minnesota. The reduced rate may tempt cowmen to ship from Mandan instead of more western points. Bad Lands Cow Boy.
1886-08-12.summary: The Northern Pacific cut livestock rates east of Mandan by an average of 50 percent, which the Cow Boy thought might draw cattle shipping to Mandan.
1886-08-12.why: Hoof and Horn (Prescott, Ariz.) of Aug 19, 1886 credits the Bad Lands Cow Boy. The item is not in the surviving Jul 1 to Aug 19 issues; it must come from one of the missing Jul 29, Aug 5 or Aug 12 issues. Aug 12 is the most recent, but Hoof and Horn often ran Cow Boy items weeks late.

1886-08-12.text: THE Bad Lands Cow Boy, just to show that it is not prejudiced against a Morton county man for member of the legislature from this district, says if H. R. Lyon will consent to run it will support him as heartily as though he was a Billings county resident. Mr. Lyon is a broad guage, fair minded man and would certainly represent the west Missouri country in an able and dignified manner.
1886-08-12.summary: The Cow Boy proposed Mandan banker H. R. Lyon for the territorial legislature and promised its support.
1886-08-12.credit: THE Bad Lands Cow Boy ... says
1886-08-12.why: Bismarck Weekly Tribune of Aug 20, 1886 reports the Cow Boy's backing of H. R. Lyon for the legislature. The surviving Aug 19 Cow Boy refers to 'Our proposal last week of H. R. Lyon's name', so the proposal first ran in the missing Aug 12 issue. The Tribune could, less likely, be summarizing the Aug 19 follow-up.

1886-09-30.text: A bunch of 200 horses were driven through Medora last Thursday evening. They will be ranged near Jamestown.
1886-09-30.summary: A band of 200 horses was driven through Medora on the way to range near Jamestown.
1886-09-30.credit: The Bad Lands Cow Boy says:
1886-09-30.why: Jamestown Weekly Alert of Oct 7, 1886 reprints this 'From Sunday's Daily' (Oct 3) crediting the Bad Lands Cow Boy. The most recent Cow Boy before Oct 3 was the missing Sep 30 issue; the surviving Sep 23 issue does not carry it.

1886-12-02.text: Bad Lands Cow Boy: A dog owned at or near Mingusville and a large buffalo wolf, have apparently formed a joint partnership for the destruction of all the choice two-year-olds and under, which graze between Mingusville and the Bad Lands. They have dragged down and partly eaten five or six head that were found by the section men, and there are doubtless many more, as yet unfound. If allowed to continue their depredations unchecked, it is not at all unlikely that they will kill $500 worth of cattle before spring. It would pay several outfits, numbers of whose cattle range on Andrew's creek, to join issues in ridding the country of these pests.
1886-12-02.summary: A dog from near Mingusville and a buffalo wolf were killing young cattle between Mingusville and the Bad Lands, and the Cow Boy urged Andrew's Creek outfits to hunt them down.
1886-12-02.why: Jamestown Weekly Alert of Thursday Dec 9, 1886 credits the Bad Lands Cow Boy; the most recent Cow Boy before it was the missing Dec 2 issue, and the surviving Nov 25 issue does not carry it.

1886-12-02.text: The butchers have gone to the new slaughter house at Kansas City.
1886-12-02.summary: The Medora butchers had left for the new slaughter house at Kansas City.
1886-12-02.credit: The following items from the Cow Boy:
1886-12-02.why: Bismarck Weekly Tribune of Dec 10, 1886 runs these under 'Medora. The following items from the Cow Boy:'. None appear in the surviving Nov 25 or Dec 9 issues, and the Dec 9 Cow Boy reports that Ellison 'left last Friday', after this future-tense notice, so the source is the missing Dec 2 issue.

1886-12-02.text: G.G. Bond will spend the winter in Boston.
1886-12-02.summary: G. G. Bond was going to Boston for the winter.
1886-12-02.credit: The following items from the Cow Boy:
1886-12-02.why: Same Bismarck Weekly Tribune Dec 10, 1886 group of 'items from the Cow Boy'; not in surviving Nov 25 or Dec 9 issues.

1886-12-02.text: J. A. Ferris bought the house of John Fitzgerald, near coal mine butte, sold at sheriff's sale.
1886-12-02.summary: J. A. Ferris bought John Fitzgerald's house near Coal Mine Butte at a sheriff's sale.
1886-12-02.credit: The following items from the Cow Boy:
1886-12-02.why: Same Bismarck Weekly Tribune Dec 10, 1886 group of 'items from the Cow Boy'; not in surviving Nov 25 or Dec 9 issues.

1886-12-02.text: The Cow Boy office has moved over the river to the Cantonement.
1886-12-02.summary: The Bad Lands Cow Boy moved its office across the Little Missouri to the Cantonment.
1886-12-02.credit: The following items from the Cow Boy:
1886-12-02.why: Same Bismarck Weekly Tribune Dec 10, 1886 group of 'items from the Cow Boy'; not in surviving Nov 25 or Dec 9 issues.

1886-12-02.text: Charles Ellison will take charge of the re-icing stations between Kansas City and New York for the Marquis de Mores.
1886-12-02.summary: Charles Ellison was to run the Marquis de Mores's refrigerator-car re-icing stations between Kansas City and New York.
1886-12-02.credit: The following items from the Cow Boy:
1886-12-02.why: Same Bismarck Weekly Tribune Dec 10, 1886 group of 'items from the Cow Boy'. The surviving Dec 9 Cow Boy says Ellison 'left last Friday for Kansas City', so this future-tense notice comes from the Dec 2 issue.

1886-12-02.text: Wm. Van Driesche has changed his plans somewhat and will make his trip to Europe before his return to Medora. Meantime, J. W. Foley will have charge of all the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car company's business here.
1886-12-02.summary: William Van Driesche would go to Europe before returning to Medora, leaving J. W. Foley in charge of the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company's Medora business.
1886-12-02.credit: The following items from the Cow Boy:
1886-12-02.why: Same Bismarck Weekly Tribune Dec 10, 1886 group of 'items from the Cow Boy'. The surviving Nov 18 Cow Boy said Van Driesche was only 'contemplating' the trip; this follow-up is not in Nov 25 or Dec 9.

1886-12-02.text: At the last meeting of the Little Missouri River Stock Growers' association it was decided that the ranges in this round-up district were fully stocked. and that in the near future notice would be given that the men here would refuse to work with any new outfits turning in cattle or horses.
1886-12-02.summary: The Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association declared the district's ranges fully stocked and planned to refuse to work round-ups with new outfits.
1886-12-02.credit: The following items from the Cow Boy:
1886-12-02.why: Same Bismarck Weekly Tribune Dec 10, 1886 group of 'items from the Cow Boy'; not in surviving Nov 25 or Dec 9 issues.

1886-12-02.text: Bad Lands Cow Boy: Owing to the number of cattle killed by trains lately in the Bad Lands the railroad compay is considering the advisability of putting on track riders between here and Glendive. So far this winter, the losses would have more than twice over paid the expenses of the riders.
1886-12-02.summary: So many cattle had been killed by trains in the Bad Lands that the Northern Pacific was considering track riders between Medora and Glendive.
1886-12-02.why: Livingston Enterprise of Saturday Dec 11, 1886 credits the Bad Lands Cow Boy. The surviving Dec 9 and Nov 25 issues do not carry it, leaving the missing Dec 2 issue.
